stem: What is the purpose of asset liability management?
options: Controlling the bank's sensitivity to changes in market interest rates and limiting losses in income and capital
Setting the bank's annual operating budget for salaries, occupancy, and technology spending
Managing each branch's cash drawers and vault limits so tellers can meet daily customer demand
Reviewing each loan application for credit risk before the loan committee approves it
why: Your notes from the review: ALM controls a bank's sensitivity to market rate changes and limits losses in income and capital (managing the balance sheet's mix of loans and deposits).

flashcard.front: What is the purpose of asset liability management?
flashcard.back: Controls a bank's sensitivity to changes in market interest rates and limits losses in income and capital

keyFact: ALM purpose: control sensitivity to market rate changes; limit losses in income and capital

stem: What is a yield curve?
options: A graph that plots the interest rates (yields) at different maturities
A graph that plots a bank's net interest margin over several quarters
A chart comparing the deposit rates competitors in your market offer
A graph that plots loan default rates at different credit scores

flashcard.back: A graph that plots the interest rates (yields) at different maturities

keyFact: Yield curve: graph of interest rates (yields) at different maturities

stem: Most of the time, the yield curve is flat.
why: Most (but not all) of the time the yield curve is upward sloping. It is only sometimes flat or inverted.

flashcard.front: True/False: Most of the time, the yield curve is flat.

keyFact: Yield curve flat most of the time: False

stem: Which of these is a type of interest rate risk (IRR)?
why: The review answer lists the IRR types: repricing risk, yield curve risk, option risk, and basis risk.

flashcard.front: What are some examples of interest rate risk (IRR)? (risk types)
flashcard.back: Repricing risk, yield curve risk, option risk, basis risk

keyFact: IRR types: repricing, yield curve, option, basis

stem: When the yield curve is upward sloping, what does that indicate?
options: Longer maturity loans or bonds are riskier than shorter term loans or bonds
Shorter term loans or bonds are riskier than longer maturity loans or bonds
The market expects interest rates to fall, as in a recession
Loans and bonds of every maturity carry about the same risk
why: Most (but not all) of the time the yield curve is upward sloping, which indicates that longer maturity loans or bonds are riskier than shorter term ones.
keyFact: Upward-sloping yield curve: longer maturity loans or bonds are riskier than shorter term

stem: A flat or inverted yield curve normally happens when the market expects interest rates to
options: Fall, for example if the economy enters recession
Rise, for example if the economy grows quickly
Stay exactly where they are for several years
Rise only at the short end of the curve
why: Sometimes the yield curve is flat or inverted. This normally happens when the market expects rates to fall, e.g. if the economy enters recession.
keyFact: Flat or inverted yield curve: market expects rates to fall (e.g. recession)

stem: Long maturity yields are largely tethered to the existing fed funds rate.
why: Short maturity yields are tethered to the existing fed funds rate. Long maturity yields reflect expectations of future economic conditions and the future path of the fed funds rate.
keyFact: Short maturity yields: largely tethered to the existing fed funds rate

stem: Net interest income (net interest margin) is the difference between
options: Interest earned on loans, investments, and cash and interest paid on deposits or borrowings
Interest earned on loans and the fees charged on deposit accounts
Total assets and total liabilities on the balance sheet
Interest paid on deposits and the bank's operating expenses
why: Banks pay interest on deposits or borrowings and earn interest on loans, investments, and cash. The difference is net interest income.
keyFact: Net interest income: interest earned (loans, investments, cash) minus interest paid (deposits, borrowings)

stem: What are the two primary factors that influence the interest rate on an individual loan?
why: Credit and maturity drive the rate on an individual loan. Macroeconomic factors like supply and demand, economic growth, inflation, and Fed policy influence all interest rates.
keyFact: Individual loan rate, two primary factors: credit and maturity

stem: A bond is typically issued with a fixed rate of interest (coupon rate) that does not change over its life.
why: The coupon is fixed, but market interest rates move up or down every day.

stem: In a bullet structure (Treasuries, agencies, munis, corporates), how often are periodic interest payments made until maturity?
why: Bullets pay interest every 6 months until maturity and return all principal at maturity.
keyFact: Bullet bonds: interest every 6 months, all principal at maturity

stem: A certificate of deposit bought as an investment can receive a federal guarantee if the investor owns less than how much of each issuer?
why: CDs are issued by banks and credit unions and can receive federal guarantee if the investor owns less than $250,000 of each issuer.
keyFact: CD federal guarantee: investor owns less than $250,000 of each issuer

stem: Which type of bond is a pool of non-mortgage assets like credit card or auto loans, where most are not guaranteed by any government entity?
why: With most ABS, the investor takes on both credit risk and prepayment risk.
keyFact: ABS: pools of non-mortgage assets (credit card, auto loans)

stem: The risk that an investor's principal will be returned earlier than expected is called
why: This normally happens when interest rates have fallen and the investor has to reinvest the proceeds into lower yielding investments.
keyFact: Call/prepayment risk: principal returned earlier than expected

stem: When a bond is bought at a discount, the discount is accreted as income.
why: Bonds priced below par sell at a discount, which is accreted as income. Bonds above par sell at a premium, which is amortized as expense.
keyFact: Bond discount: accreted as income (premium is amortized as expense)

stem: When market yields decrease, bond prices also decrease.
why: Yield and price move in opposite directions: yields decrease, price increases; yields increase, price decreases.
keyFact: Yield and price: move in opposite directions

stem: What is the maturity range of a Treasury Note?
why: Treasury bills mature in up to 1 year, notes in 1 to 10 years, and bonds in more than 10 years.
keyFact: Treasury Note maturity: 1 to 10 years

stem: What risk-based capital weighting does a municipal revenue bond carry?
why: Revenue bonds carry 50% risk-based capital weighting. General obligation bonds carry 20%.
keyFact: Municipal revenue bond risk-based capital: 50% (GO bonds 20%)

stem: A municipal bond for a water and sewer utility is secured by the revenue stream of that project. What type of municipal bond is it?
why: Revenue bonds are secured by the revenue stream of the project. General obligation bonds are backed by the government's authority to levy taxes.

stem: Which mortgage-backed securities carry the full faith and credit of the US, so the holder assumes no credit risk?
why: GNMA guarantees pools of FHA, VA, and RHS loans with the full faith and credit of the US (0% RBC). FNMA and FHLMC carry an implicit guarantee (20% RBC).
keyFact: GNMA MBS: full faith and credit of the US, 0% risk-based capital

stem: Which of these is NOT one of the 3 primary funding sources?
why: The 3 primary funding sources are deposits, cash flows / loan renewals, and the Fed / wholesale funding.

stem: Which ALM component is the decision making body that manages the ALM processes?
why: Policy states management's ALM objectives, measurements are the ratios and analyses, software calculates them, and ALCO makes the decisions.
keyFact: ALCO: decision making body that manages the ALM processes

stem: The ALCO is primarily concerned with interest rate risk management issues.
why: ALCO duties include pricing, profitability, cash flow needs, and managing risk, but it is primarily concerned with interest rate risk.

stem: Which of these is NOT one of the types of interest rate risk?
why: The types of interest rate risk listed are repricing risk, yield curve risk, option risk, and basis risk.
keyFact: Types of interest rate risk: repricing, yield curve, option, basis

stem: Economic Value of Equity (EVE) is a short-term model used for the 12 and 24 month time horizon.
why: EVE and extended income simulation are long-term models (longer than 24 months). Gap analysis and income simulation are the short-term models.
keyFact: Short-term IRR models (12 and 24 months): gap analysis and income simulation

stem: If a bank is liability sensitive, its net interest income will move in the same direction as interest rates.
why: A liability sensitive bank's liabilities reprice faster than its assets, so net interest income moves opposite to rates. An asset sensitive bank's NII moves the same direction.
keyFact: Liability sensitive bank: NII moves opposite to interest rates

stem: A bank has a negative GAP and interest rates increase. What happens to its net interest income?
options: It increases because interest income rises
why: With a negative gap, interest expense rises more than interest income when rates go up, so net interest income decreases.
keyFact: Negative GAP, rates increase: net interest income decreases

stem: How is Economic Value of Equity (EVE) calculated?
options: Present value of all asset cash flows less present value of all liability cash flows
Total book value of assets less total book value of liabilities
Interest income less interest expense over the next 12 months
Rate sensitive assets less rate sensitive liabilities in each time bucket
why: EVE captures the change in economic value of the bank even when that change isn't reflected in the accounting books.
keyFact: EVE: PV of all asset cash flows less PV of all liability cash flows

stem: Who is ultimately responsible for the interest rate risk (IRR) of the institution?
why: The board approves the IRR or A/L policy and risk limits. Senior management executes the board-approved strategies.
keyFact: Ultimately responsible for IRR: Board of Directors
